en: Very skilled or proficient at something
hook: ADEPT: an ADEPT is an ADEPT-ed expert.
story: Nadia's grandmother is adept at bargaining; within two minutes she can get the fish seller to drop his price by half, and he still smiles. Adept means highly skilled. Synonyms: proficient, adroit, deft. Be adept at time management on the GRE.

en: Harmful or unfavorable
hook: ADVERSE: like an ADVERSARY, working against you.
story: The new medicine had adverse side effects: headaches, nausea, and dizziness. Adverse weather also delayed the flight by five hours. Adverse means harmful or unfavorable. Don't confuse it with averse, which means unwilling: I'm averse to adverse conditions.

en: Suitable or proper for the situation (adj.); to take something for one's own use, often without permission (verb)
hook: Two pronunciations: ap-PRO-pree-it means SUITABLE; ap-PRO-pree-ate means to TAKE as your PROPERTY.
story: Wearing a white sari to the funeral was appropriate; it suited the occasion. But the manager who appropriated company funds for his new car was arrested. As an adjective, appropriate means suitable. As a verb, to appropriate means to take something for yourself, often without permission. The GRE tests both.

en: A very typical example; an original model
hook: ARCH-TYPE: the ARCH (chief, first) TYPE.
story: The wise old grandmother who tells stories by the fire is an archetype found in folk tales across the world. Sherlock Holmes is the archetype of the brilliant detective. An archetype is the original pattern or perfect example. Synonyms: prototype, exemplar.

en: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively; to express clearly
hook: ARTICULATE: every ARTICLE of speech placed perfectly.
story: In the interview, Mitu was articulate: she explained her research in simple words, answered every question clearly, and never rambled. She was offered the job on the spot. Articulate means able to express ideas clearly. As a verb, to articulate is to put thoughts into words.

en: Showing signs of future success; favorable
hook: AUSPICIOUS: AUSPICES were bird signs Romans read for good luck.
story: Rafi's new shop opened on Pohela Boishakh, an auspicious day for new beginnings. By evening, he had sold everything. Auspicious means promising good fortune. An auspicious start suggests a successful future. Synonym: propitious.

en: Deprived of something valuable; lacking
hook: BEREFT: BEREAVED, left without.
story: After the fire, the family was bereft of everything: home, clothes, and photos. The politician's speech was bereft of any new ideas. Bereft means deprived or lacking. Bereft of hope means having lost all hope.

en: Tending to find fault over trivial things
hook: CAPTIOUS: tries to CAPTURE you in tiny errors.
story: The captious reviewer complained about a comma in chapter three, a slightly wrong date in chapter seven, and the font on the cover, but said nothing about the brilliant story. Captious means fault-finding over small things. Synonyms: carping, nitpicking.

en: Proving something beyond doubt
hook: CONCLUSIVE: brings the argument to a CONCLUSION.
story: The fingerprints on the knife provided conclusive evidence; there was no longer any doubt about who committed the crime. Conclusive means decisive and final. GRE passages often note that evidence is suggestive but not conclusive.

en: To secretly plan to do something harmful; to combine to produce a result
hook: CON-SPIRE: breathing (spire) together in whispers.
story: Two employees conspired to steal company data and sell it to a rival. Later, rain, traffic, and a flat tire conspired to make Arif late for his exam. To conspire is to plot secretly, or for events to combine against you.

en: To describe or portray precisely; to mark the boundary of
bn: সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে বর্ণনা করা; সীমা নির্ধারণ করা
hook: DE-LINE-ATE: draw the LINES clearly.
story: Before starting the project, the manager delineated everyone's responsibilities: who handles design, who writes code, who talks to clients. No confusion remained. To delineate is to describe precisely, or to outline borders on a map.

en: To free from something that is tangled or complicated
hook: DIS-ENTANGLE: undo the TANGLE.
story: Sara spent twenty minutes disentangling her earphone wires. Later, the lawyer disentangled the complicated property dispute between four brothers. To disentangle is to separate or free from complexity. Synonyms: extricate, unravel.

en: To strongly urge someone to do something
hook: EX-HORT: like a coach shouting 'HURT now, win later!'
story: Before the final, the captain exhorted his team: 'Play for your families, play for your country, give everything!' To exhort is to urge strongly and passionately. Synonyms: urge, implore, encourage.

en: Physical weakness; moral weakness
hook: FRAILTY: being FRAIL.
story: In his last years, Grandpa's frailty was heartbreaking; he could barely walk to the veranda. Shakespeare wrote, 'Frailty, thy name is woman,' about moral weakness. Frailty means weakness, physical or moral. Human frailty includes greed, envy, and pride.

en: A real or imagined cause for complaint
hook: GRIEVANCE: something that makes you GRIEVE and complain.
story: The workers listed their grievances: unpaid overtime, broken toilets, and no fire exits. They demanded a meeting with management. A grievance is a complaint about unfair treatment. Holding grievances for years poisons relationships.

en: A long, loud, aggressive speech; to lecture at length
hook: HARANGUE: HARASS with a long rant.
story: The landlord delivered a twenty-minute harangue on the tenants' doorstep about wet clothes on the balcony. Nobody could get a word in. A harangue is a loud, long, scolding speech. Synonyms: tirade, diatribe.

en: A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage
hook: PLOY: a PLOT to deceive.
story: The 'fifty percent off' sign was just a ploy; the shop had doubled prices the week before. A ploy is a clever trick to gain an advantage. Synonyms: stratagem, gambit, ruse.

en: Graceful, calm, self-controlled manner
hook: POISE: perfectly POISED, balanced and calm.
story: When her microphone failed during the national debate, Nadia kept her poise, smiled, raised her voice, and continued without missing a beat. Poise means calm composure and grace under pressure.

en: Self-important, overly formal behavior or speech
hook: POMPOSITY: POMP and show of importance.
story: The new officer's pomposity annoyed everyone: he insisted on being called 'Honourable Sir,' gave long speeches about his own achievements, and used big words to say small things. Pomposity is pretentious self-importance. Pompous is the adjective.

en: A person authorized to act for another; a substitute
hook: PROXY: like a PROXY attendance a friend gives for you in class.
story: Unable to attend the shareholders' meeting, Mitu's father sent his lawyer as his proxy to vote on his behalf. In research, test scores are often used as a proxy for intelligence, though imperfectly. A proxy is a substitute or representative.

en: To finally agree after refusing; to become less severe
hook: RELENT: finally LET it go.
story: Tanvir's parents refused to let him travel alone. After weeks of pleading, they finally relented, on one condition: he must call every night. To relent is to give in after resisting. The rain finally relented in the evening.

en: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; sometimes, language that is impressive but insincere
hook: RHETORIC: a RHETORICAL question doesn't need an answer — it's just for effect.
story: The politician's rhetoric was powerful: big promises, emotional stories, and catchy slogans. But voters noticed that none of it came with real plans. Rhetoric is persuasive language, sometimes empty. Studying rhetoric helps you analyze GRE arguments.

en: Strictness, thoroughness, and accuracy; harsh conditions
hook: RIGOR: RIGID standards.
story: The research program was famous for its rigor: every claim checked twice, every experiment repeated three times. Graduates were respected everywhere. Rigor means strict precision. Rigorous is the adjective. The rigors of winter are its harsh conditions.

en: Thinly scattered; small in number or amount
hook: SPARSE: SPARE, very little.
story: In the desert, vegetation was sparse: a few dry bushes, miles apart. The audience at the early-morning lecture was sparse too, just six students in a hall for two hundred. Sparse means thinly scattered. Synonyms: scant, meager.

en: Resolutely firm and loyal
hook: STEAD-FAST: holding FAST to your place (stead).
story: Through her husband's long illness, she remained steadfast: by his side every day for five years, never complaining. Steadfast means firmly loyal and unwavering. A steadfast friend never leaves. Synonyms: stalwart, resolute.

en: Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality
hook: GRE trick: SUSPECT as an adjective means questionable.
story: The study claiming that chocolate improves exam scores was suspect; it was funded by a chocolate company. On the GRE, suspect as an adjective means questionable or untrustworthy. Suspect evidence shouldn't convince anyone.

en: Too long, slow, or dull; tiresome
hook: TEDIOUS: like TED talking forever.
story: Copying two hundred pages of handwritten notes into a computer was tedious work; after an hour, Rafi's eyes and fingers ached. Tedious means boring and tiresome. Synonyms: monotonous, humdrum, wearisome.

en: The state of being strong and energetic
hook: VITALITY: VITAL life energy.
story: At eighty, Grandma's vitality amazed everyone: morning walks, gardening, cooking for twenty, and dancing at weddings. Vitality means energy and liveliness. A city's vitality shows in its markets, music, and crowded streets.

en: Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses
hook: WHIMSICAL: full of WHIMS.
story: The café had whimsical decorations: teacups hanging from the ceiling, chairs painted like animals, and a menu written as a poem. Whimsical means playful and fanciful, sometimes unpredictable. A whimsical decision is made on impulse.

en: To produce or provide; to give way under pressure
hook: YIELD has two meanings: PRODUCE (a crop yields rice) and GIVE WAY (a yield sign).
story: This year, the field yielded a record harvest of rice. But when the strong wind came, the old bamboo fence yielded and fell. To yield means to produce, or to give way. At a yield sign, you give way to other cars.
